These counts stay pinned where they are rather than dropping to zero; see GATES.md ABANDON: P2-G4 and DEBT-REGISTER.md. This file was written after the other twelve were documented, which is why it carried the decision without stating it.
__reason.src/lib/price.ts: Five lines, and none of them is interface copy: they are the LEXICON a Hebrew price sheet actually prints. `שח`, `ש"ח`, `שקל`, `דולר`, `אירו` and `יורו` are tokens this parser has to recognise in a supplier's spreadsheet cell, alongside `₪`, `$`, `€` and `£`. They must match what the SUPPLIER wrote, never what the reader's interface language happens to be -- moving them into a dictionary would make an English-locale session stop recognising a shekel sign, which is the opposite of a fix. The parser's own refusal messages are translation KEYS and carry no Hebrew at all (0298, Wave 2).
__reason.src/lib/bankImportWorkbook.ts: Twelve lines stay: the Hebrew guide sheet and the worked example row of the bank-import template (EXP-09). They are written INTO public/templates/inplace-bank-import-v1.xlsx, never onto a screen, and this module is a pure workbook writer with no locale to consult -- the same class as workbook.ts and reportTemplateExport.ts. The asset is served from one fixed URL for every locale (Bank.tsx downloadTemplate), so there is no reader whose language could be asked at the moment the bytes are written; a locale-aware template would mean generating the file in the browser instead of serving the static one, which changes what that button does. Known consequence, stated rather than hidden: an English-locale reader downloads a Hebrew guide sheet. The strings live HERE rather than only in scripts/generate-bank-import-assets.mjs so bankImportWorkbook.spec.ts can compare the shipped file against the module cell for cell -- a generator whose output nothing compares is how a template and its parser drift apart.
